newsitem.title: USA: Pemex Cactus blast leaves winter propane shortfall.
newsitem.headline: Pemex Cactus blast leaves winter propane shortfall.

text.p: Petroleos Mexicanos (Pemex) will have to return to the international propane market to meet winter demand because of the gap between supply and demand left by the July blast at its largest gas-processing plant at Cactus, market players said this week.
The shortfall is expected despite a recent contract with Saudi Arabia for 500,000 barrels per month of supply from September to March, analysts and U.S. traders said.

Mexican commercial and residential demand for propane, largely thought to have been satisfied by the Saudi barrels, is expected to increase by an estimated 420,000 barrels a month with the December approach of the winter heating season.

"In the best case scenario Pemex will need about 14,000 more barrels per day," said LPG analyst Dan Lippe, of Petral Consulting Co. "There is no winter demand in Mexico until December and then it increases to a peak usually in January."
The need for extra barrels is despite news that Pemex recently restarted two units at the Cactus plant that were undamaged in the July 26th blaze.

The portion is estimated by Lippe and another U.S. analyst (who didn't want attribution) to comprise about two-thirds, or 100,000 barrels of LPG, of the total LPG production capacity of the Cactus complex.
Though a Pemex source said Wednesday the restarted units brought the Cactus complex up to 80 percent of its pre-explosion capacity, a number of U.S. market players doubt it could be that high.
"Given the amount of gas (300 mcf a day) that Pemex is still importing, I would be surprised to hear if it is at 80 percent production capacity," said the analyst who requested to remain anonymous.
"I don't know how much they are lacking in propane, but with the upcoming winter season they will have to meet some more needs," the analyst added.

Although Mexico's domestic demand for propane is not readily available, analysts note that propane is a major feedstock used by petrochemical companies as well as the dominant cooking and heating fuel for most residential homes.
The big question for traders, however, is which market Pemex will bite into.

Petral's Lippe said it is possible the monopoly will focus on the U.S. Gulf Coast, where Pemex ships will be docking to load on the Saudi barrels for transfer to its draft-restricted (shallow) Los Parajitos port.
Pemex's three vessels have a combined capacity to transport an extra 570,000 barrels per month on top of the monthly 500,000 barrel Saudi supply, said Lippe.
One Houston-based international broker, however, reckons the U.S. market will be too expensive for Pemex given the 25-year-record lows for U.S. propane inventories, which have driven up prices.
"They've got some serious problems at Cactus. I would expect Pemex to start buying about 500,000 more barrels per month starting the first quarter.
"Right now the U.S. is too expensive. They might sell some barrels in Belvieu to hedge against cargoes they buy (at lower prices) internationally," he added.

Some traders said they have already seen Pemex selling in the U.S. market, but are unsure whether this is, as Pemex maintains, because it is long or as part of a strategy to lower the cost of extra imports it will need.
A Pemex source based in Houston says his company is long supply and has been looking for buyers in the U.S. and Latin America. He denies Pemex will need more imports later int he year.
"We don't need any more propane," said the Pemex source. "We have a long position right now and want to sell some of our supply."
One thing however, is clear. Should Pemex come again into the U.S. market -- assuming there is enough supply -- it will pressure up prices already at extraordinarily high levels.
-- NY Energy Desk 212-859-1631
